Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to push them out of my mind

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported violent trauma. Hospital smells and loss-related conversations fit, but weapons/object-as-weapon cues are clinically implausible for the same index trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'You can never know who will harm you' implies interpersonal danger/assailant threat, which is poorly matched to the validated trauma of a child's serious illness. This also aligns awkwardly with the rest of the profile, which is otherwise illness/loss/moral injury themed rather than assault-based.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Intense rage on recall' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for an 80-year-old mother traumatized by a child's life-threatening illness. The other items center on helplessness, permanent change, loss-related and hospital triggers, and intrusive affect without image. Distress, fear, guilt, grief, or sadness would fit more coherently; rage is not impossible, but here it is insufficiently supported by any corresponding appraisal or trigger content and stands out as clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands
issues.explanation: 'Cover face with hands' is not well supported as a maladaptive strategy in this profile. The active formulation links maladaptive strategies mainly to negative appraisals and memory, and the other strategies chosen (avoid going out, thought suppression) fit intrusive distress and negative beliefs. Face hiding is more typical of acute shame/panic/social exposure and is not clearly connected to the hospital/loss triggers, intrusive memory pattern, or appraisals provided, making it the least coherent item in this set.

vignette:
Layla, an 80-year-old widow and retired social worker of Middle Eastern descent, still lives in the apartment she shared with her late husband. The trauma that reshaped her life was not a single violent moment but a slow, agonizing ordeal: her son's childhood leukemia diagnosis and the two years of treatment that followed. He survived, now a healthy man in his fifties, but for Layla, the event never ended. She can still feel the full, suffocating weight of the grief she felt standing in the hospital corridor, the antiseptic smell so thick it seemed to coat her tongue, even though no clear image of that moment comes to mind-only the emotion, raw and undimmed, as if her body had forgotten the picture but kept the feeling. The memory forces its way into her mind when she least expects it, often triggered by something as simple as the scent of rubbing alcohol in a doctor's office or a passing comment on the news about someone losing a loved one. When this happens, the overwhelming grief she felt back then returns, and she is left feeling helpless, certain that she has permanently changed for the worse, that the woman she was before the illness is gone forever.

These triggers do more than just bring the memory back; they also reinforce her deepest negative appraisals. Every time she smells a hospital or sees a needle, she is flooded not only with grief but with the conviction that she acted in ways that go against who she is-that she was too frightened, too weak, too consumed by her own panic to be the mother her son needed. She had come to believe that she cannot stop bad things from happening, and each triggered episode only deepens that belief, making her feel even more helpless and damaged. This appraisal, in turn, makes her hypervigilant to any potential trigger in her environment, scanning for the next olfactory or visual cue that might confirm her worst fears about herself. She now avoids going out unless absolutely necessary, and when she does, she takes circuitous routes to steer clear of the hospital district. She has also learned to suppress the thoughts when they intrude, trying to push them out of her mind, though this effort often leaves her feeling more exhausted and more convinced of her own permanent damage. The maladaptive strategy of avoidance-refusing to see a doctor for her own aches and pains, canceling appointments, ignoring routine health screenings-has only deepened her sense of helplessness, creating a loop where her actions confirm her worst appraisals. The memory itself, when it intrudes, strengthens her belief that she is irreparably broken, and that belief makes the next memory more likely to surface, as she remains on constant alert for any sign of failure.

The most dominant connection in her experience is the one she feels tightening every day: the memory triggers her negative appraisals, and those appraisals trigger the memory in turn, a closed circuit with no exit. She will be sitting quietly, and the grief will rise unbidden; then the thought follows, I failed him, I am not the same person, I am helpless, and that thought alone is enough to summon the memory again, as if her mind is proving her right. She has come to believe that she is a permanent victim of her own past, and this belief has cost her. She no longer visits her son's family as often, fearing that a stray comment about a sick friend or a child's fever will pull her back into that hospital room. Her daughter-in-law has noticed, and Layla knows she has hurt them, but the shame of that only adds to her sense of permanent damage.

What finally brought her to seek help was not the grief itself, but the realization that she had not been to a doctor in four years, even as her own body began to ache. She is terrified of what she might find, but she is also terrified of what she has become: a woman who cannot bear to walk past a hospital, who cannot talk about loss without collapsing, who has let her own trauma slowly erase her from her family's life. She is hoping, more than anything, to find a way to feel like herself again-though she is not sure she remembers who that is.
